messages.author: 53876b6270ad9337
messages.subject: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
parts:
Hello ggploters,

Are there any comprehensive examples of using grid to show multiple
plots side by side in the same graphic? I've had very little luck
finding a good example of something like:

[Plot1][Plot2][Plot3]

Thanks,

BEB

messages.author: 4c2460918214ec91
messages.subject: Re: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
parts:
Hi -

In Hadley's book there is the standard example. (~p.153)
The following isnt comprehensive (since it's not reproducible), but I believe you'll be able to make sense of it (and in the doc i was currently working on). Note that you can also use ranges in vplayout, eg vplayout(1,2:3). Also i've left ggplot() to mean whatever you need to plot, not an actual command, since i'm not using any supplied data.

---------------------------
vplayout <- function(x,y)
  viewport(layout.pos.row=x,layout.pos.col=y)

overall <- ggplot( )
ts.fraction <- ggplot( )    
continent.fraction <- ggplot()
duration.fraction <- ggplot()    
area.fraction <- ggplot( )    
magnitude.fraction <- ggplot()    

pdf('heavy_rain_floods.pdf',width=11,height=8.5)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(3,2)))

print(overall,vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(ts.fraction, vp=vplayout(1,2))
print(continent.fraction, vp=vplayout(2,1))
print(duration.fraction, vp=vplayout(2,2))
print(area.fraction, vp=vplayout(3,1))
print(magnitude.fraction, vp=vplayout(3,2))

dev.off()

Best, 

James

messages.author: 9ff02ee016b8a9e0
messages.subject: Re: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
parts:
Another option may be to use the function 'arrange' below. For example, 

myplot1 <- ggplot(dataframe,aes(x=variable,=y=variable)) + geom_point()
myplot2 <- ggplot(dataframe,aes(x=variable,=y=variable)) + geom_point()
arrange(myplot1,myplot2,ncol=1) # you can specify ncol and nrow as well


# Function used below in the function 'arrange'

vp.layout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)


# Function to plot multiple ggplots together

arrange <- function(..., nrow=NULL, ncol=NULL, as.table=FALSE) {

 dots <- list(...)

 n <- length(dots)

 if(is.null(nrow) & is.null(ncol)) { nrow = floor(n/2) ; ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}

 if(is.null(nrow)) { nrow = ceiling(n/ncol)}

 if(is.null(ncol)) { ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}

        ## NOTE see n2mfrow in grDevices for possible alternative

grid.newpage()

pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(nrow,ncol) ) )

 ii.p <- 1

 for(ii.row in seq(1, nrow)){

 ii.table.row <- ii.row

 if(as.table) {ii.table.row <- nrow - ii.table.row + 1}

  for(ii.col in seq(1, ncol)){

   ii.table <- ii.p

   if(ii.p > n) break

   print(dots[[ii.table]], vp=vp.layout(ii.table.row, ii.col))

   ii.p <- ii.p + 1

  }

 }

}



SAC

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
parts:
Hi:

There was a thread last spring that concerned this topic. Here's an example I drummed up at the time; the idea was to use theme_blank() to remove the plot.background. I also messed around with the viewport centers manually. See below for another approach.

# Generate a Brownian motion series
df <- data.frame(t = 1:1000, y = cumsum(rnorm(1000)))
rg <- range(df$y)
fn <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0, floor(x), ceiling(x))
rg <- sapply(rg, fn)

# Idea is a time series plot with a rotated histogram next to it
# p is the time series plot, q is the rotated histogram
# in q, cut out the xlab and value labels
p <- qplot(x = t, y = y, data = df) + ylim(rg[1], rg[2])
q <- qplot(x = y, data = df) + coord_flip() +
           xlim(rg[1], rg[2]) +
           opts(axis.text.y = theme_blank()) + xlab('')

# strip off the plot backgrounds to pull plots closer together
p2 <- p + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())
q2 <- q + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())

# Create some viewports
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.25, height = 1, x = 0.875, y = 0.5)
vp3 <- viewport(width = 0.85, height = 1, x = 0.425, y = 0.5)

# The first pair of plots has overrunning space; the second
# pair does not. The x11() window works on my Win7 box;
# if it doesn't work, try another device.

x11(7, 3.5)
print(q, vp = vp2)
print(p, vp = vp3)

grid.newpage()
print(q2, vp = vp2)
print(p2, vp = vp3)
dev.off()
#------------------------

Fernando also contributed to that thread, and his approach used plot.margin instead. This is the part I kept, so some context may be lost:

######### Fernando's example using opts(plot.margin) ##########

p <- q <- qplot(1, 1) + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())

# View graphs before the margins are altered
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1, 2)))
print(p, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(q, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))

# left margin negative compensated with a larger right margin
# to maintain the proportions of the plot [aspect ratio]
q <- q + opts(plot.margin = unit(c(1, 3, 0.5, -2.5), "lines"))

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1, 2)))
print(p, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(q, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))

Fernando's method is more robust than mine, since it fine tunes the parameters rather than hunting and pecking to fit.

HTH,
Dennis
